market_context: United States; NOAA/USDA/NIH reference data with the state of each reference made explicit
title: Hake vs. salmon: protein, fat, calories, and omega-3

seo.title: Hake vs. salmon: protein, fat, calories, and omega-3
seo.meta_description: Raw hake is roughly 65–90 calories and 1–2 g fat/100 g; salmon is about 180–210 calories and 10–13 g fat. Protein is much closer than fat.
seo.search_intent: Compare hake and salmon for protein, fat, calories, and omega-3 while keeping raw versus cooked reference states explicit.

excerpt: Hake and salmon can provide similar amounts of protein in a serving, but their energy profiles are very different. Hake is lean; salmon carries roughly 10 g more fat per 100 g and far more EPA and DHA.
content_html:
Hake and salmon both work as protein-rich seafood, but they represent two different styles of fish. Protein can be fairly close; fat and calories are where the gap becomes much larger.

A practical comparison per 100 g

NutrientHakeSalmon
Calories~65–90 kcal in raw references~180–210 kcal in fresh references
Protein~12–18 g depending on species/data~18–22 g
Fat~1–2 g~10–13 g
Omega-3roughly a few tenths of a gram in hake referencesoften ~1.8–2.2 g EPA+DHA/100 g in cooked Atlantic salmon references

The calorie, protein, and fat rows allow a reasonable comparison across fresh or raw references. The omega-3 row does not pair two analyses in an identical state; it is included to show the order-of-magnitude difference, so the cooked state of the salmon reference is stated explicitly.

NOAA lists 90 calories, 18.31 g protein, and 1.31 g fat per 100 g raw red hake. European hake entries can be closer to 65 calories and 12 g protein. That spread is a reminder that species and data source belong next to the number.

The major difference is fat

If hake provides 1.5 g fat and salmon 12 g per 100 g, salmon contains about 10.5 g more fat. That difference alone represents roughly 95 calories.

This explains much of the calorie gap. It does not mean salmon is automatically a worse choice; it means equal weights contribute differently to total energy intake.

Across a 5-ounce serving, that fat gap can approach 15 grams. Once cooking oil, sauces, or sides are added, the finished meal changes again, so the fish itself should not be separated from preparation when comparing total calories.

Protein is much closer

A hake entry with 18 g protein and a salmon entry with 20 g differ by only 2 g per 100 g. Across a 5-ounce serving, that is roughly 25.5 versus 28.4 g protein.

Even a hake entry near 12 g protein/100 g is only 6–10 g below the 18–22 g salmon range, while fat can differ by roughly 9–12 g and energy by about 90–145 calories/100 g.

That makes protein a weak reason to choose one over the other. Both can anchor a protein-rich meal; fat, omega-3 content, taste, price and availability create larger practical differences.

Salmon clearly provides more EPA and DHA

NIH lists 1.83 g EPA+DHA in a 3-ounce serving of cooked farmed Atlantic salmon. Hake is not omega-3-free, but lean white fish contains much less long-chain omega-3 than fatty salmon. Those figures are not an identical-state laboratory comparison, so they should be read as a difference in scale rather than as a perfectly controlled head-to-head measurement.

Salmon's extra fat is therefore not simply “extra calories.” A meaningful share includes the long-chain omega-3s that are one of salmon's nutritional strengths. Hake's very low fat is what makes it such a lean fish.

Do not compare raw hake with cooked salmon without saying so

Cooking removes water. That can raise protein and calories per 100 g even when no nutrients are added. A chart that compares raw hake with grilled salmon therefore mixes a cooking effect into the species comparison.

Added fat matters too. A lightly oiled grilled fillet is different from deep-frying or serving the fish with a rich sauce. For a fair food comparison, match preparation as closely as possible and then account for recipe ingredients separately.

Which one makes more sense?

If you want a very lean option, hake is around 1–2 g fat and 65–90 calories/100 g in raw references; if you prioritize EPA and DHA, cooked Atlantic salmon references are often around 1.8–2.2 g/100 g.

They do not need to compete for one permanent place in the diet. Alternating them provides different strengths.

Hake works especially well when you want a lean protein and prefer to add olive oil, nuts, or a more energy-dense side yourself. Salmon brings more fat and omega-3 to the plate, so it may need less added fat to remain rich and satisfying.

The useful takeaway

Hake and salmon are far closer in protein than in fat. Hake is often around 1–2 g fat per 100 g, while salmon is commonly around 10–13 g. That extra fat raises calories but also carries much of salmon’s EPA and DHA.

faq.question: Which has more protein, hake or salmon?
faq.answer: It depends on species and preparation. In comparable references they can be fairly close, often within the broad 18–22 g per 100 g range.

faq.question: Which has fewer calories?
faq.answer: Hake. Raw references are often about 65–90 calories per 100 g compared with roughly 180–210 for fresh salmon references.

faq.question: Which has more omega-3?
faq.answer: Salmon by a wide margin. Hake contains some omega-3 but is a much leaner fish; when comparing exact numbers, keep the raw or cooked state visible.
